idiom_name: hand-written Map[Class[_], Any] locator, or a framework injector such as Play's instanceOf[T]
implementation_notes: Scala's own type-directed facility resolves at compile time, not run time: givens with summon[T] and context bounds are how a Scala 3 program obtains collaborators, which is why a runtime locator is a smell here rather than a pattern. Where a runtime lookup is genuinely required it is hand-written - a Map[Class[_], Any] or Map[String, () => Any] built at the composition root, read back with a ClassTag-typed get that throws on an unknown key - or borrowed from a framework: Play exposes Injector.instanceOf[T] (Guice-backed by default) for components Play itself constructs, and java.util.ServiceLoader covers class-path discovery. Keep application code on constructor parameters and givens, and confine the locator to reflection-driven or framework-created code.
pitfalls: ClassTag-based keys erase type parameters, so Repository[User] and Repository[Order] collide on one key; Scala's givens or explicit qualifiers are the fix (Koin and Guice need named/qualified bindings for the same reason).
asInstanceOf is unchecked: registering the wrong value throws ClassCastException at the consumer rather than at startup.

Under Scala 3 prefer summon[A]/context parameters; keep the Map registry for code the compiler cannot see (reflection-driven frameworks, plugin loading) and treat Play's injector as framework infrastructure, not as application architecture.
